questions.q: What does torch.utils.tensorboard.SummaryWriter require that wandb does not?
options: A paid subscription
Nothing extra — SummaryWriter writes local log files and requires no external account or API key, unlike a hosted service
An internet connection at all times
A GPU to function at all
questions.explain: SummaryWriter is part of PyTorch itself and writes log files locally, which the tensorboard command then serves as a dashboard — no external account or service required, unlike hosted tools like wandb.

questions.q: What is the main practical advantage of wandb.init(config={...}) over just logging scalar metrics?
options: It makes training run faster
It permanently attaches the run's hyperparameters to that run, making it searchable and filterable later (e.g. by learning rate)
It replaces the need to call wandb.log() during training
It automatically fixes bugs found during training
questions.explain: Passing config to wandb.init() records the hyperparameters for that specific run, so you can later filter or compare runs by their configuration instead of relying on memory or old scripts.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when does it make the most sense to move from TensorBoard to a hosted tool like Weights & Biases?
options: Immediately, for every project, regardless of scale
Never — TensorBoard should always be preferred
Once comparing many runs by eye across separate local views stops scaling, or once multiple people need to view the same results
Only when training on a CPU instead of a GPU
questions.explain: TensorBoard is free, local, and sufficient for a lot of solo work. A hosted tool becomes more valuable once you're running enough experiments that comparing them manually stops being practical, or once collaboration is involved.

questions.q: What habit does this lesson emphasize as the thing that actually makes experiment tracking useful?
options: Logging as many metrics as possible, regardless of relevance
Logging hyperparameters/config alongside metrics, not metrics alone
Only logging the final loss value at the end of training
Avoiding any logging until training is fully complete
questions.explain: A loss curve with no record of what configuration (learning rate, batch size, etc.) produced it becomes much less useful once you're trying to compare it against other runs later.

questions.q: What command serves the TensorBoard dashboard from logs written by SummaryWriter?
options: python -m tensorboard.serve
wandb sync
tensorboard --logdir <log_dir>
torch.utils.tensorboard.launch()
questions.explain: After SummaryWriter has written logs to a directory, running `tensorboard --logdir <that directory>` from a terminal starts the local dashboard that reads and displays them.
